subject: history
title: Henry VIII and the Break with Rome
welcome_lead: Annulment, supremacy and dissolution: how England left the Roman Church.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on Henry VIII, Thomas Cromwell and the English Reformation.
final_note: You have followed the king from defender of the faith to supreme head.

concepts.def: Henry VIII's campaign (1527-33) to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon.
1533 statute by Cromwell declaring England an empire and barring appeals to Rome.
1534 Act declaring Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England.
Chief minister 1532-40 who engineered the Reformation legislation and Dissolution of the Monasteries.
Suppression of religious houses 1536-40, transferring lands and wealth to the crown.
1536 northern uprising led by Robert Aske protesting religious changes and dissolution.

walkthroughs.h2: Why did Henry break with Rome?
walkthroughs.body_html: Catherine of Aragon failed to produce a male heir and Henry desired marriage to Anne Boleyn. Pope Clement VII, under Imperial pressure after Charles V's 1527 sack of Rome, refused annulment. Cromwell engineered a parliamentary solution: the 1533 Act in Restraint of Appeals and 1534 Act of Supremacy severed papal jurisdiction, making Henry head of the Church.

Cromwell's 1535 Valor Ecclesiasticus valued monastic wealth. Smaller houses were suppressed in 1536, larger ones by 1540. Land was sold to gentry and nobles, creating vested interests in Reformation continuity. The crown gained an estimated GBP 1.3 million but squandered much on war; the social landscape was permanently altered.

A.G. Dickens argued the Reformation reflected genuine Protestant feeling and anticlericalism. Revisionists such as Eamon Duffy in The Stripping of the Altars (1992) presented vibrant traditional religion overturned by state coercion. The 1536 Pilgrimage of Grace, with 30,000 marchers, suggests significant northern resistance to imposed change.
